newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss bank, prosecutor say no documents withheld.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bank, prosecutor say no documents withheld.

text.p: Swiss prosecutors and Union Bank of Switzerland on Wednesday rejected claims by a former watchman that Holocaust-era files he saved from shredding at the bank were more extensive than UBS had disclosed.

UBS, the country's biggest bank, stuck by an announcement it made on Monday that the documents were records of 31 properties held by a subsidiary bank in Germany, including three whose previous owners might have been Jewish.
"We have very detailed information and this is what we published," UBS spokeswoman Gertrud Erismann told Reuters.
Former watchman Christoph Meili told a news conference the documents he had rescued from the shredder room in fact listed 45 properties, all of which he said were Jewish-owned.

Historians probing Switzerland's World War Two role have said documents on Jewish properties sold in Germany in the 1930s may provide clues to how much Swiss businesses profited from the Nazi policy of seizing, or "Aryanising", Jewish holdings.
Zurich prosecutor Peter Cosandey, who is investigating both UBS and Meili in the shredding case, backed up the bank's version of how many documents Meili took.
"The bank's statement (on Monday) was accurate. There were certainly not 45 properties," Cosandey said.
The documents made world headlines when Meili made them public in January, saying he had taken them from a shredder room at UBS in Zurich.
Jewish groups campaigning to make Swiss banks open their records of assets left by Holocaust victims accused UBS of deliberately trying to get rid of evidence.

Zurich prosecutors are investigating whether Meili broke bank secrecy laws and whether UBS violated a federal decree that prohibits destruction of any records relevent to a sweeping historical probe of Switzerland's World War Two role.
UBS called the shredding a regrettable mistake and said the records from Eidgenoessische Bank, a Swiss bank it bought in 1945, bore no relation to customer accounts.

UBS this week released a detailed breakdown of the records, saying they comprised 65 files on properties in Germany including 47 documents from the period before and during World War Two and 18 from the 1950s, 60s and 70s.

Bankers said Meili appeared to be counting most of the pre-1945 documents as records of separate properties, rather than ignoring duplicates, and assuming that all were formerly owned by Jews before the Eidgenoessische Bank bought them.
On Tuesday, Meili showed reporters a list of what he said were more than 45 Jewish-owned properties from the 1930s to 1945.

"UBS did not tell the truth about these documents and still is not telling the truth about the documents they destroyed and what I found," Meili told reporters at the offices of his Manhattan attorney Edward Fagan.
The 28-year-old also charged that UBS had failed to disclose information from other documents he saved.
These showd wartime loans to German companies, documents about German chemical and submarine manufacturing companies, and the ledger sheets of German companies with bank accounts in Swiss banks.

Meili fled to the United States from Switzerland with his wife and two young children in April, saying he felt his life was in danger. The U.S. Congress has called him a hero and offered him special fast-track residency permission.
